title: Parts of plant and animal cells
keyIdea: Every living thing is made of cells, and each part of a cell has a job. Animal and plant cells both have a cell membrane (controls what goes in and out), cytoplasm (where most reactions happen), a nucleus (holds the DNA and controls the cell), mitochondria (release energy from glucose in respiration) and ribosomes (make proteins). Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall for strength, a permanent vacuole full of sap that keeps the cell firm, and, in green parts, chloroplasts that absorb light for photosynthesis. Root cells have no chloroplasts because they get no light.
familyTip: Make a cell model in a sandwich bag: jelly or hair gel for cytoplasm, a grape for the nucleus, raisins for mitochondria and sprinkles for ribosomes. For a plant cell, put the bag in a small box (the wall) and add a water balloon (the vacuole) and green peas (chloroplasts). Ask: which parts would a root cell leave out?

visual.caption: Which cells have this part? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: build an animal cell, a leaf cell and a root cell, match six jobs to their parts, zoom a microscope to ×400 and fill a vacuole.

kid: All living things are made of cells. A cell is the smallest living unit. Each part inside it has a job, a bit like rooms in a house.

Plant and animal cells share five parts. The cell membrane is a thin skin. It controls what goes in and out. The cytoplasm is a jelly where most reactions happen. The nucleus holds the DNA and controls the cell. Mitochondria release energy from glucose. Ribosomes make proteins.

Plant cells have three extra parts. A cell wall made of cellulose makes the cell strong. A big vacuole full of sap pushes out and keeps the cell firm. Chloroplasts trap light to make food. But only green parts have them. Root cells live in the dark, so they have none.
Most parts are too small to see by eye. A light microscope at ×400 shows the wall, the nucleus and the chloroplasts. Ribosomes are far smaller. You need an electron microscope to see them.
adult: Ages 11 to 12. The KS3 biology course in England says cells are the basic unit of life. Pupils learn what the cell wall, membrane, cytoplasm, nucleus, vacuole, mitochondria and chloroplasts do. They compare plant and animal cells and use a light microscope. Ribosomes are added because the topic lists them and GCSE needs them.

Key facts. The membrane lets some things through and not others. The cellulose wall lets almost all through, but stops the cell bursting. The vacuole holds sap and keeps the cell firm. Chloroplasts hold chlorophyll for photosynthesis. Mitochondria are where respiration releases energy from glucose. Ribosomes make proteins. The nucleus holds the DNA. Total magnification is eyepiece times objective: ×10 and ×40 give ×400. Ribosomes need an electron microscope.

Common mistakes: giving animal cells a wall; saying plants have no mitochondria because chloroplasts 'do the energy'; thinking all plant cells are green; giving the wall the membrane's job; saying mitochondria make energy; and adding lens powers instead of multiplying. Each has its own feedback in the lab and the challenge.

practice.prompt: Which part controls what enters and leaves a cell?
practice.hint: It is the thin, flexible layer every cell has.
practice.explain: The cell membrane controls what passes in and out. The cell wall is strong but lets almost everything through.

practice.prompt: A microscope has a ×10 eyepiece and a ×{o} objective lens. What is the total magnification? (Type the number.)
practice.hint: Multiply the eyepiece by the objective.

practice.prompt: A leaf cell has {n} chloroplasts. A root cell from the same plant is about the same size. How many chloroplasts does the root cell have? (Type the number.)
practice.hint: Does light reach a root under the soil?
practice.explain: 0. Root cells get no light, so they have no chloroplasts, however many the {n}-chloroplast leaf cell has.

practice.prompt: Which three parts do plant cells have that animal cells do not?
choices: Cell wall, permanent vacuole and chloroplasts
practice.hint: Animal cells have no wall, no big vacuole and cannot photosynthesise.
practice.explain: Plant cells add a cellulose wall, a permanent vacuole and chloroplasts. Both kinds share the nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm, mitochondria and ribosomes.

practice.prompt: What is the job of the mitochondria?
choices: Release energy from glucose in respiration
practice.hint: Every cell needs energy, plant or animal.
practice.explain: Mitochondria release the energy stored in glucose by aerobic respiration. Chloroplasts make the glucose; the vacuole stores sap.

pool.prompt: Which part do animal cells NOT have?
pool.hint: What is the outer layer of an animal cell?
pool.explain: Animal cells have no cell wall; their outer layer is the membrane. They do have mitochondria.

pool.hint: Do plants need energy at night?
pool.explain: Yes. Plant cells respire all the time, so they need mitochondria. Chloroplasts make glucose; mitochondria release its energy.

pool.prompt: Where is a cell's DNA kept?
pool.hint: Which part controls the cell's activities?
pool.explain: The nucleus holds the DNA in chromosomes. The genes control what the cell does.

pool.prompt: An image is magnified ×{=10*o} using a ×10 eyepiece. What power is the objective lens? (Type the number.)
pool.hint: Total = eyepiece × objective, so divide the total by 10.

pool.prompt: Why does a plant wilt when it is short of water?
choices: Its vacuoles shrink, so the cells go floppy
pool.hint: What keeps a plant cell firm?
pool.explain: Full vacuoles press the cytoplasm against the wall and keep cells firm. With less water the vacuoles shrink and the plant wilts.

pool.prompt: A leaf cell has {k} mitochondria and {c} chloroplasts. How many of these parts release energy from glucose by respiration? (Type the number.)
pool.hint: Chloroplasts make glucose. Which part releases its energy?
pool.explain: Only the {k} mitochondria release energy by respiration. The {c} chloroplasts make glucose by photosynthesis.

pool.prompt: Which can you see clearly with a school light microscope at ×400?
pool.hint: Which of these parts is the biggest, and big enough to show at ×400?
pool.explain: The nucleus is big enough to see at ×400. Ribosomes and the inside of mitochondria need an electron microscope.

pool.prompt: Which part absorbs light for photosynthesis?
pool.explain: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light to make glucose by photosynthesis.
